# Module 2 Assignment Exercises

## 1) Moving Average Smoothing of Australian Overnight Trips

For this exercise, we will use the the `tourism` dataset from the the `tsibble` package.

### a. Replace the plot below using 2x12-MA smoothing over the entire series \[remove the `.png` file from your submission\].

```{r aus_tourism-plot}
#| warning: false
# Load Tourism data
data(tourism)

# Calculate 2x12-MA for the entire series
tourism_ma <- tourism |>
  summarize(Trips = sum(Trips)) |>
  mutate(
    `12-MA` = slider::slide_dbl(Trips, mean,
      .before = 5, .after = 6, .complete = TRUE),
    `2x12-MA` = slider::slide_dbl(`12-MA`, mean,
      .before = 1, .after = 0, .complete = TRUE)
  )

# Plot 2x12-MA
tourism_ma |>
  autoplot(Trips, colour = "gray") +
  geom_line(aes(y = `2x12-MA`), colour = "maroon") +
  labs(y = "Trips (thousands)", title = "Overnight Trips - Australia")
```

### b. Create a table showing values for each quarter in 2015

Your table should be well formatted and suitable for a publication or presentation. It should contain

- The Quarter identifier
- The actual \`Trips\` value (suitably scaled and labeled)
- The smoothed Trips values
- The delta between actual and smoothed

```{r aus_tourism-table}
# Create professional table
tourism_ma |>
  filter(year(Quarter) == 2015) |>
  mutate(Delta = Trips - `2x12-MA`) |>
  select(Quarter, Trips, `2x12-MA`, Delta) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Australian Overnight Trips (2015)**"),
             subtitle = "Actual vs. 2x12-MA Smoothed Values") |>
  tab_spanner(label = "Overnight Trips (in Thousands)",
              columns = c(Trips, `2x12-MA`, Delta)) |>
  cols_label(Quarter = "Quarter", Trips = "Actual",
    `2x12-MA` = "2x12-MA Smoothed", Delta = "Delta (Actual - Smoothed)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Trips, `2x12-MA`), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = Delta, decimals = 2, force_sign = TRUE) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(80), latex.tbl.pos = "H")

```

## 2) Forecasting Australian Wine Sales : Exponential Smoothing

The figure below shows time plots of monthly sales of six types of Australian wines (red, rose, sweet white, dry white, sparkling, and fortified) for 1980-1994. Data available in AustralianWines.xls. The units are thousands of liters.

```{r ch5_fig}
# Reproduce the textbook
aus_wine <- read_csv(here::here("data/AustralianWines.csv"), na = "*",
                     col_types = cols(Rose = col_number()),
                     show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
    fill(Rose, .direction = "down") |> 
    mutate(Month = mdy(str_replace(Month, '-', '-01-')) |> yearmonth()) 

aus_wine |> 
    pivot_longer(cols = -Month, names_to = 'Varietal', values_to = 'Sales') |> 
    ggplot(aes(Month, Sales)) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap(~ Varietal, scales = "free_y") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Fortified wine has the largest market share of the six types of wine. Focus on fortified wine sales alone and produce as accurate a monthly forecast as possible for the next year.

### a) Create an autoselected exponential smoothing model

- Start by partitioning the data using the period until December 1993 as the training period.
- Create an exponential smoothing model allowing `ETS()` to autoselect the model type.
- Output the model information

```{r ets_auto}
# Create a time series object for fortified wine sales (tsibble)
fortified <- aus_wine |> 
    select(Month, Fortified) |>
    as_tsibble(index = Month) 

# Create training/validation sets for the model
fortified_trn <- fortified |>
    filter_index(. ~ '1993 Dec')  

# Fit an ETS model
fit <- fortified_trn |>
  model(ETS(Fortified))

# Output raw model information
report(fit)
```

```{r ets_auto pt2}
# Output the model information
tidy(fit) |>
  filter(term %in% c("alpha", "beta", "gamma")) |>
  mutate(Parameter = case_when(
      term == "alpha" ~ "Alpha (Level smoothing)",
      term == "beta"  ~ "Beta (Trend smoothing)",
      term == "gamma" ~ "Gamma (Seasonal smoothing)")) |>
  select(Parameter, Estimate = estimate) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**ETS(M, A, M) Model Parameters**"),
    subtitle = "Fortified Wine Sales (Training Period: 1980–1993)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = Estimate, decimals = 4) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(70), latex.tbl.pos = "H")
```

### b) Interpret the model and parameters that ETS() selected as the optimum

- The auto ETS determined that the best combination of methods were multiplicative errors, additive trend, and multiplicative seasonality. Multiplicative seasonality indicates that seasonal swings scale with the overall fortified wine sales volume, while the additive trend indicates a consistent change in sales over time.

- Alpha represents the smoothing parameter for level, which is how quickly weights diminish with older data. This value of alpha (0.0243) is very small which indicates higher smoothing. This means recent observations are not tracked aggressively, so the model filters out short-term noise and relies more on the long-term historical baseline.

- Beta represents the trend's smoothing parameter, which is how frequently trend is allowed to change. The value (0.0011) is very low, which means the trend does not change often.

- Gamma represents the smoothing parameter for seasonality, which is how frequently seasonal patterns are allowed to change. The value (0.0001) is very low meaning that seasonality does not change often.

### c) repeat the modeling step with an autoselect model, an Additive Holt-Winters model with additive errors and any other model of your choice. Report the RMSE, MAE and MAE for each model. Sort the report from best to worst based on `AICc`

```{r ets_multi}
# Set seed for reproduceability
set.seed(123)

# Fit multiple models
fit <- fortified_trn |>
  model(
    auto = ETS(Fortified),
    hw = ETS(Fortified ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("A")),
    mhw = ETS(Fortified ~ error("A") + trend("A") + season("M")),
    `damp mhw` = ETS(Fortified ~ error("A") + trend("Ad") + season("M"))
  )

# Output metrics
glance(fit) |>
  select(Model = .model, AICc) |>
  left_join(
    accuracy(fit) |> select(Model = .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE),
    by = "Model") |>
  arrange(AICc) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**Model Accuracy**"),
    subtitle = "Fortified Wine Sales (Training Period: 1980–1993)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AICc, RMSE, MAE), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = MAPE, scale_values = FALSE, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), latex.tbl.pos = "H")
```

- I reported on MAE and MAPE, the prompt for question 2c lists MAE twice, so I interpreted this to mean MAE and MAPE.

- The dampened multiplicative Holt-Winters and Additive Holt-Winters did not outperform in any metric. The Multiplicative Holt-Winters has the lowest MAPE (6.98%) and the lowest RMSE (278.59), but the Auto model (ETS(M, A, M)) showed the lowest AICc (2,757.60), making it the best model considered in this set when looking at training performance.

### d) Create a plot with just the last year of the training data (1993) that shows the fitted values for each model overlaid on top of the training (actual) data.

```{r ets_fit-plt}
# Create the 1993 Actual vs. Fitted plot
fit |>
  augment() |>
  filter(year(Month) == 1993) |>
  autoplot(.fitted) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = Fortified, linetype = "Actuals"),
    colour = "black",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_yearmonth(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Fitted Sales for Fortified Wine (1993)",
    subtitle = "Comparing ETS models during the final year of training data",
    x = "Month (1993)",
    y = "Sales (thousands of liters)"
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = NULL),
    linetype = guide_legend(title = NULL)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### e) Forecast the data for each month of 1994 for each model and compare the resulting metrics.

- Report MAE, RMSE, and MAPE for all models, ordered by best RMSE.
- Present your results in a well formatted table (suitable for presentation).

```{r ets_results}
# Set seed again for reproduceability
set.seed(123)

# Forecast the validation period 
forecast_1994 <- fit |>
  forecast(h = "12 months")

# Review accuracy to select the best model
forecast_1994 |>
  accuracy(fortified) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  select(Model = .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**1994 Out-of-Sample Forecast Accuracy**"),
    subtitle = "Evaluation of all ETS models against actual 1994 sales"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(RMSE, MAE), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = MAPE, scale_values = FALSE, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(80), latex.tbl.pos = "H")
```

Which model produces the best mean forecast? Did all the metrics agree with each other?

- The auto ETS model produces the best forecast because it has the lowest RMSE (318.90), MAE (242.65), and MAPE (10.24%).

- Interestingly, the Additive Holt-Winters has the second best RMSE (337.18), but the worst MAE (280.58) and MAPE (12.24%), meaning that the metrics do not always agree with one another and must be prioritized properly to decide on the best model (if auto ETS were not included).

### f) Use the best performing model to create a forecast for each month in 1995.

- Fit a model against the full dataset.
- Forecast the next year of data.
- Create a plot showing forecast values and intervals (80%, 95%) for 1995 alongside actual values from 1990 onwards.

```{r ets-fc-plt}
# Use the full data set to fit the best model
fit <- fortified |>
  model(auto = ETS(Fortified))

# Forecast the next 12 months
forecast_1995 <- fit |>
  forecast(h = "12 months")

# Plot the forecast
forecast_1995 |>
  autoplot(fortified |> filter(year(Month) >= 1990)) + 
  labs(
    title = "Best Model (Auto ETS) 1995 Forecast of Sales by Month",
    y = "Sales (thousands of liters)"
  )
```

### g) Output the mean forecast values for 1995

```{r ets-fc-table}
# Produce 1995 forecast table
forecast_1995 |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, `Mean Forecasted Fortified Wine Sales` = .mean) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**1995 Mean Forecasted<br>Fortified Wine Sales by Month**")
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `Mean Forecasted Fortified Wine Sales`, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(70), latex.tbl.pos = "H") |>
  tab_source_note(
    source_note = md("*Note:* Mean Forecast reported in thousands of liters.")
  )
```

### h) Create a time plot of the residuals from your last model

```{r ch5-8c}
# Obtain residuals
residuals <- fit |>
  augment()

# Plot Residuals
autoplot(residuals, .resid) +

       y = "Sales (thousands of liters)")
```

## 3) Forecasting Australian Wine Sales: Time Series Regression

- Use your existing partitioned data (training through December 1993).
- Fit a regression model to sales with a linear trend and seasonality.

### a) Create the "actual vs. forecast" plot for the next 12 months.

- Include actual data from 1990 for comparison
- Show the default prediction intervals

```{r fortified-tslm-plt}
# Reusing the training data from the previous question

# Fit a TSLM model to the training set 
fit_tslm <- fortified_trn |>
  model(TSLM(Fortified ~ trend() + season()))

# Forecast the validation period
forecast_1994 <- fit_tslm |>
  forecast(h = "12 months")

# Plot the forecast
fortified |>
  filter(year(Month) >= 1990) |>
  autoplot(Fortified) +
  autolayer(forecast_1994, alpha = 0.5) + 
  labs(
    title = "TSLM (Trend + Season) Forecast for Fortified Wine (1994)",
    y = "Sales (thousands of liters)"
  )
```

**What can you say about the model fit?**

- The 1994 forecast captures the seasonal shape well, but certain months over or under forecast actual values because the TSLM seasonality is additive while ETS seasonality is multiplicative, giving it an advantage compared to TSLM.

- Generally speaking, actual sales values are included in the prediction intervals, but there are some months where the actual sales are outside of the prediction interval, indicating poor model fit, especially compared to ETS.

### b) Compare the TSLM and best ETS models for the validation period

- (Hint) It may be easier to create a new `mable` object by refitting the data
- Compare the RSME, MAE and MAPE metrics for each model in a well formatted table (suitable for presentation). Sort from best to worst RMSE.

```{r fortified-compare}
# Create a new mable object with just the two models we want to compare
fit <- fortified_trn |>
  model(
    auto = ETS(Fortified),
    tslm = TSLM(Fortified ~ trend() + season())
    )

# Forecast the validation period
forecast <- fit |>
  forecast(h = "12 months")

# Compare the model accuracies
forecast |>
  accuracy(fortified) |>
  arrange(RMSE) |>
  select(Model = .model, RMSE, MAE, MAPE) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = md("**1994 Out-of-Sample Forecast Accuracy**"),
    subtitle = "Auto ETS vs. TSLM against actual 1994 Fortified Wine sales"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(RMSE, MAE), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_percent(columns = MAPE, scale_values = FALSE, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(80), latex.tbl.pos = "H")
```

### c) Produce a forecast for all wine types for sales in all months of 1995 using a linear regression model. Your forecast should be in the form of a presentable table with wine varietals as columns and months as rows.

```{r ch6-6c}
# Create a tsibble for all the wine types
wines_ts <- aus_wine |> 
    pivot_longer(cols = -Month, names_to = 'Varietal', values_to = 'Sales') |> 
    as_tsibble(index = Month, key = Varietal) 

# Fit the series
fit <- wines_ts |>
  model(TSLM(Sales ~ trend() + season()))

# Forecast the series
forecast <- fit |>
  forecast(h = "12 months")

# Use pivot wider to shape the output
forecast |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(Month, Varietal, .mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Varietal,
              values_from = .mean) |>
  rename(`Dry White` = `Dry white`,
        `Sweet White` = `Sweet white`,
        Sparkling = sparkling) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("**1995 TSLM Sales Forecast by Varietal**"),
             subtitle = "Mean Forecast reported in thousands of liters.") |>
  fmt_number(decimals = 2) |>
  cols_align(align = "center") |>
  opt_stylize(style = 1) |>
  tab_options(table.width = pct(100), latex.tbl.pos = "H")
```

## 4) Reflections

a\. What was the most challenging part of this assignment?

- Question 2a presented the greatest challenge for me, I had to consult the text to ensure I was interpreting the alpha, beta, and gamma coefficients properly.

b\. What is the most important takeaway from this assignment?

- Properly designing tables is one of my most important takeaways from this assignment. I had not used great tables (`gt`) before, I was vaguely aware of kable, but overall I was impressed how much control the library enabled me to have over table styling. I am normally not great with designing tables, but it was relatively easy to pick up once I had some practice.

- My second most important takeaway was how much better ETS was compared to TSLM in question 3b, and in question 3a I summarized why I believe ETS was better suited for that specific task compared to TSLM.

c\. What would you recommend changing for future courses?

- No recommendations, I think this assignment was a good step up from assignment 1, and I thought it was an appropriate challenge.

d\. What LLMs did you use (if any) to help you complete this assignment?

- I used Gemini to help me learn great tables syntax and provide feedback on problems after I took a first and second pass over them. I consulted the text first to ensure I did not rely too heavily on Gemini.
